cards.front: What bonding feature makes all six carbon–carbon bonds in benzene equal in length?
cards.back: **Delocalisation**: the sideways overlap of six p orbitals forms a ring of six delocalised electrons, so every C–C bond lies between single and double bond length.
cards.hint: Think about what the fourth outer electron on each carbon atom does.

cards.front: Why does benzene release less energy on hydrogenation than three separate double bonds would?
cards.back: **Delocalisation** gives benzene extra stability, so it starts at a lower energy and releases less energy when hydrogenated.
cards.hint: Compare benzene's starting energy with three isolated double bonds.

cards.front: Why does benzene not decolourise bromine water, unlike alkenes?
cards.back: Its electron density is **spread over six carbons**, so it is lower between any two atoms and does not attract bromine. Addition would also destroy the delocalised ring.
cards.hint: Compare where the electron density sits in a C=C bond with where it sits in the ring.

cards.front: Why is it wrong to draw benzene with alternating double and single bonds?
cards.back: **All six C–C bonds are identical**, with electrons shared evenly round the ring. The bonds do not switch between double and single.

cards.front: Using hydrogenation values of $-208$ and $-120\,\mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}$, how much more stable is benzene than the Kekulé structure predicts?
cards.hint: Start by multiplying cyclohexene's value by three.

cards.back: A species that **accepts a pair of electrons** to form a covalent bond, often a positive ion.
A reaction in which an **electrophile replaces an atom**, usually hydrogen, on a ring, so the delocalised ring is kept in the product.
cards.hint: Contrast it with the addition reactions of alkenes.

cards.front: What is the nitronium ion and what is its formula?
cards.back: The **cation $\mathrm{NO_2^+}$**, the electrophile that attacks benzene in nitration. Sulfuric acid protonates nitric acid, then water is lost to form it.

cards.front: What are the steps of the nitration mechanism once the nitronium ion has formed?
cards.back: 1) The ring donates a pair of electrons to $\mathrm{NO_2^+}$, forming a C–N bond and a positive intermediate. 2) The C–H bond breaks and **H+ leaves**. 3) H+ combines with $\mathrm{HSO_4^-}$ to re-form $\mathrm{H_2SO_4}$.
cards.hint: Start with what the benzene ring does to the electrophile.

cards.front: Why must nitration be kept at no more than $50\,^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$?
cards.back: Hotter mixtures give products with **more than one nitro group**, so the reaction must stay controlled to make nitrobenzene.
cards.hint: Consider what further nitration does to the product.

cards.front: What is the acylium ion and what is its formula?
cards.back: The cation **$\mathrm{RCO^+}$**, formed when aluminium chloride removes chloride from an acyl chloride. It is the electrophile in acylation.
cards.hint: Think about what $\mathrm{AlCl_3}$ does to the acyl chloride.

cards.front: Why is aluminium chloride described as a catalyst in Friedel–Crafts acylation?
cards.back: It is **regenerated** at the end of the mechanism, so it is not used up and does not appear in the overall equation.

cards.front: What is the organic product when benzene is acylated with ethanoyl chloride?
cards.back: **Phenylethanone**, $\mathrm{C_6H_5COCH_3}$, a ketone: its carbonyl carbon is bonded to two carbon groups.
cards.hint: Think about which functional group the new acyl group creates on the ring.

cards.back: A **hydrocarbon** whose molecules contain one or more benzene rings.
